text: Full and differential backups are both snapshots of data pages. A transaction log backup is categorically different — and that difference is the whole reason point-in-time recovery exists at all.

A full or differential backup is a photograph of what the database's storage looked like at one moment. A log backup is a record of every transaction since the last one, in the order they happened. Restoring only full and differential backups can only put you back at a moment one of them happened to run. Replaying log backups on top lets you stop at any exact second in between.

For a healthcare scheduling and billing database, that's not academic. Restore to last night's backup could mean losing an entire day of real appointments and payments. Restore to 2:35 p.m., one minute before a bad script ran, is a fundamentally better answer — and only the log backup chain makes that possible.

Consistent with the last two lessons, there's no BACKUP LOG statement to write here. Azure SQL Database takes transaction log backups automatically, every 5 to 10 minutes, continuously — tighter, in fact, than the 15-minute interval Lesson 2 planned by hand. That means Overlook's database already has an even smaller real-world recovery point objective than the original plan called for, at no extra engineering cost.

Right now, underneath Overlook's database, Azure has everything it needs to restore to nearly any point in the last several minutes. Next lesson, you'll actually use that chain — picking a real point in time and watching the restore happen.
